tagline: River roads connect sandstone canyons, a bluff-top drive and an ancient mound.
intro: The Illinois River Road follows rolling hills and river towns between Ottawa and Havana, using a network of roads on both banks. The Illinois Office of Tourism describes a 291-mile National Scenic Byway linking more than 100 nature-based destinations, with Havana 150 miles south of Ottawa. Its account emphasizes state parks, wildlife refuges and river-valley views; at Peoria, Grandview Drive winds for 2.52 miles above the valley. At Peoria Heights, the landscape can be roughly divided into river floodplain, bluff and plateau.

Grandview’s construction tells one part of the road network’s story. Peoria’s park board began planning the drive and securing land rights in 1896. Landscape gardener and engineer Oscar F. Dubuis developed its plan in 1902, trying to preserve the original trees. Work began in 1903 with hand labor and horses. Cars later left the gravel-and-sand surface dusty and rutted; asphalt replaced it in the mid-1930s.

Travel south from Ottawa to Starved Rock’s canyons, then through the Hennepin and Lacon stretch of the river valley toward Peoria. Grandview Drive supplies the bluff views before the journey continues toward Chautauqua National Wildlife Refuge and Havana. At Havana, Rockwell Mound marks a settlement history reaching back two thousand years.

moments.title: Starved Rock State Park
moments.text: Starved Rock’s sandstone cliffs and canyons show what water can do to poorly cemented rock. A flood from a melting glacier, the Kankakee Torrent, helped shape the terrain. The park has 18 deep canyons and more than 13 miles of hiking trails. Its name comes from a local siege legend involving the Illiniwek, Ottawa and Potawatomi; the Wikipedia park history finds no historical evidence for the siege beyond oral history. Illinois bought the former resort in 1911 and opened the state park to the public in 1912. French, LaSalle, Ottawa and St. Louis canyons have the park’s longer-lasting waterfalls.

moments.title: Grandview Drive
moments.text: The river side of Grandview Drive remains largely park-district land, undeveloped except for benches. Across the road, historic houses form a residential district added to the National Register in 1996. The drive’s plan sought to retain original trees, including oaks, hickory, maples and sycamore. A five-story observation tower completed in 1906 was demolished in 1942 because of corrosion and repair costs. Its metal went to the World War II scrap effort. The winding drive runs between Prospect Road and Illinois Route 29, with several places set aside for taking in the view.
moments.notice: River-valley views lie opposite historic houses along Grandview Drive.

moments.title: Havana
moments.text: Rockwell Mound gives Havana a history much older than its river ferry. The earthen mound dates to around AD 200, covers almost two acres and rises about 12 feet. A Potawatomi village occupied the site when English-speaking residents arrived in 1822. A ferry crossed to the western bank of the Illinois River, connecting with a road that followed the Spoon River. In 1858, Abraham Lincoln gave a three-hour Senate-campaign speech on the mound, one day after Stephen Douglas spoke there. The settlement was first called Ross’s Ferry before taking the name Havana, after Cuba’s capital.
